commitResults.messageTitle: Added new banner, changed bot name to Bibi. Updated greetings.
Level-0 completed
Implemented necessary changes for level 1
Implemented add to list feature
Implemented a new Task class, made modules to handle Task completion logic
Added functions to write a ToDo task type
Implement inherited Level 4 task types and UI testing
Implemented exceptions for level 6 requirements
Implemented remove function
[joshmode] iP
Save tasks to disk whenever the task list changes
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 7 requires the task list to survive between sessions. This first step
covers writing only; reading the file back follows in the next step.

Storage owns the save file and writes one line per task in the documented
T | 1 | read book format. The path is built with Paths.get("data", "bibi.txt")
so it stays relative to the project root and works on any operating system,
and the data folder is created on demand for a fresh copy of the project.

Encoding lives with the tasks themselves: Task.toFileFormat() writes the shared
type, status, and description fields, and each subclass supplies its own extra
fields through the new getSaveFields() hook. This mirrors how getDetails()
already works, so adding a task type later needs no change to Storage.

Bibi saves after every add, mark, unmark, and remove. A failed save is reported
but does not end the session, since the in-memory list is still usable.

The UI test runner now resets data/bibi.txt before each case, because saved
tasks would otherwise leak from one case into the next. It also understands a
<<restart>> marker and a "Saved data" block so later cases can exercise loading.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Load saved tasks when Bibi starts
commitResults.messageBody:
Second step of Level 7: Bibi now reads data/bibi.txt at startup, so a session
continues from where the previous one ended.

Storage.parseTask splits a line on the field separator and rebuilds the task
through the normal Todo, Deadline, and Event constructors, which means the same
validation that guards typed input also guards loaded input. A missing save
file is treated as an ordinary first run and produces an empty list rather than
an error, since the file will not exist on someone else's computer.

Bibi confirms how many tasks were restored, and stays silent when there are
none so a first run is not cluttered.

Test plan gains three cases: tasks surviving a restart, a first run with no save
file, and restoring a file written earlier.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle save file errors and corrupted data
commitResults.messageBody:
Third step of Level 7, covering the stretch goal. Before this change a single
damaged line crashed Bibi on startup with an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Loading now checks each line before trusting it: the field count must match the
task type, the status flag must be 1 or 0, and the type code must be known.
A line that fails any check is skipped with a numbered explanation while every
other task still loads, and blank lines are ignored. Storage.load returns a
LoadReport so it can hand back both the tasks and the warnings without printing
anything itself. A file that is not readable text, or a path that is not a file
at all, is reported the same way instead of ending the program.

Task text is now rejected when it contains '|', because such text would be
split into the wrong fields when read back and would silently corrupt the file.
Deadline and Event validate their times through the same helper as the
description, which also removes the duplicated blank checks.

Failed saves name the file and the kind of error, so a problem such as the data
folder being blocked by a file of the same name is easy to diagnose.

Test plan gains a corrupted-file case and a case for the rejected separator.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-7'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 7: Bibi saves the task list to ./data/bibi.txt after every change and
loads it again at startup, handling a missing file, a missing folder, and
corrupted content.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store deadline and event times as real dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 8 minimal requirement: dates are now understood as dates rather than kept
as whatever text the user typed.

The new TaskDateTime class holds a LocalDate plus an optional LocalTime, and
owns all parsing and formatting. The time is optional rather than defaulted to
midnight, so "/by 2019-10-15" stays a whole-day deadline and only prints a time
when one was actually given. Input accepts yyyy-MM-dd and d/M/yyyy, each with an
optional 24-hour time, which covers the "2/12/2019 1800" example from the brief.
Display uses MMM dd yyyy, with the locale fixed to English so month names do not
change with the machine's regional settings.

The saved form (2019-12-02 or 2019-12-02 1800) is also an accepted input format,
so the save file stays readable and editable by hand and needs no separate
parser.

Holding real dates makes a check possible that plain text could not support:
an event is now refused if it would end before it starts.

Task gains occursOn(LocalDate), answering false by default since a ToDo has no
date. Deadline and Event override it, which prepares for the "on" command.

Note that a save file written by the previous version, holding free text such as
"Sunday", no longer loads. Those lines are reported through the Level 7
corrupted-line handling and skipped, rather than being silently accepted.

Test plan updated to use real dates, plus cases for the accepted formats,
rejected dates, and an out-of-date save file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add an on command to list tasks for one date
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 8 stretch goal: "on <date>" reports the deadlines due that day and the
events running that day.

The search is asked of the tasks themselves through occursOn, so Bibi does not
need to know which types carry dates. An event counts as occurring on any day
between its start and end, so a multi-day event is found on its middle days too,
and a ToDo is never matched because it has no date.

Matches keep the number they have in the full list rather than being renumbered,
so a task found this way can be marked or removed straight away without a
further list command.

Any time of day in the query is ignored, since the question is about the whole
day. An unreadable date is refused with the same guidance as elsewhere.

The welcome text, help text, and unknown-command hint now mention the command
and the date formats, and the test plan covers a matching date, a date with
nothing on it, and an unreadable one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-Level-8'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 8: deadlines and events store real dates and times through the new
TaskDateTime class, are displayed as MMM dd yyyy, and can be queried for a
single date with the on command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Ui class for all console interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
First step towards the A-MoreOOP target. Bibi was the only class that touched
System.in and System.out, and that responsibility is now Ui's.

Ui owns the mechanics of the conversation: the "You: " prompt, the divider
lines, the "Bibi: " prefix, task numbering, and the fixed screens (welcome,
help, goodbye). Wording specific to one operation is still passed in by the
caller, so adding a command later does not mean adding a method to Ui. That
keeps Ui from becoming a dumping ground of one method per message while still
making it the single place that writes to the console.

Two small fixes came with the move:

- Reaching the end of the input now counts as "bye" instead of throwing
  NoSuchElementException. Piped input that omits a final bye no longer crashes.
- markTask and unmarkTask dropped a null check on the result of findTask, which
  can never be null because findTask throws instead.

Behaviour is otherwise unchanged, which the 15 UI tests confirm.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Give Storage and TaskList clearer responsibilities
commitResults.messageBody:
Second step towards A-MoreOOP, preparing for the Parser and Command classes.

Storage now reads and writes plain List<Task> instead of TaskList. Saving and
loading files has no reason to know how the running program holds its tasks, and
the narrower interface means Storage can be tested with an ordinary ArrayList.

TaskList gains a constructor that takes an existing list, so a loaded file
becomes a task list in one step rather than by adding tasks one at a time. The
tasks are copied, so the caller's list cannot be changed underneath it.

The save-file location moved out of Storage and into Bibi, which is the class
that composes the application. Storage no longer decides where it lives, it just
uses the path it is given, and there is a single place to look for the path.

Behaviour is unchanged; the 15 UI tests confirm it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace the command if-else chain with Parser and Command classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Third step of A-MoreOOP, covering the stretch goal in the same move because the
Parser has to return something, and a Command is the natural thing to return.

Parser now owns every command word and its syntax, and hands back a finished
Command. It resolves arguments while parsing, so "deadline ... /by ..." becomes
a built Deadline and "mark 2" becomes an int. A command can therefore assume its
input is already sound and has no parsing left to do.

Command is abstract with execute(tasks, ui, storage) and isExit(). The nine
subclasses are Add, List, Mark, Unmark, Delete, On, Help and Exit. AddCommand
covers all three task types because Parser has already built the task, so no
separate AddTodoCommand and friends are needed.

Saving after a change lives in Command.saveTasks, so the four commands that
change the list all save the same way and report a failed save the same way,
without failing the command itself.

Bibi is now an object rather than a bag of static methods. It holds ui, storage
and tasks, and run() is the short loop from the target design. Loading happens
in run() rather than the constructor because it speaks to the user and the
greeting should come first.

Two visible changes:

- Divider lines are now printed once per command by the loop, instead of by each
  operation. Commands that previously showed none, such as mark and errors, are
  now wrapped consistently.
- "help" works on its own. The old router only matched "help " with a trailing
  space, so bare "help" fell through to the unknown-command message. Writing
  that special case back deliberately made no sense while rewriting the
  dispatch, since every other command word matches both forms.

All 16 UI tests pass, including a new one pinning the help output.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreOOP'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-MoreOOP: extract Ui, Parser and a Command hierarchy alongside the existing
Storage and TaskList, so Bibi only wires the parts together and runs the loop.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organize classes into bibi, bibi.task and bibi.command packages
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Packages, taking the stretch goal since eighteen classes are more than one
folder should hold.

The split follows the roles established in A-MoreOOP:

- bibi: Bibi, Ui, Parser, Storage, BibiException. The application itself and the
  parts that connect it to the outside world.
- bibi.task: Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, TaskList, TaskDateTime. What a task is
  and how a collection of them behaves, with no knowledge of console or files.
- bibi.command: Command and its eight subclasses. What the user can ask for.

src/main/java stays the source root, and the folders under it mirror the package
names, as the increment requires.

bibi.task came out of this as the only package that depends on nothing but
BibiException, which is a good sign the boundary is in the right place. The
bibi and bibi.command packages do depend on each other, since Parser builds
commands while commands need Ui and Storage. That cycle is inherent to the
Command pattern here and is not worth breaking with extra interfaces at this
size.

Members already had the visibility they needed, so no access modifiers changed:
the protected hooks on Task are only used by its subclasses in bibi.task, and
everything reached across a package boundary was already public.

The UI test runner now compiles recursively and runs bibi.Bibi, and the README
points at the new location of the main class. All 16 UI tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Packages'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Packages: classes organised into bibi, bibi.task and bibi.command, with
src/main/java kept as the source root.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'add-gradle-support'
Point the Gradle build at this project and document it
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Gradle. The add-gradle-support branch merged cleanly into this branch, since
the Duke.java it carries was already deleted along our own history, so nothing
had to be resolved by hand.

Two settings had to change for the build to describe this project rather than
the template:

- application.mainClass is bibi.Bibi, the packaged main class from A-Packages.
- shadowJar produces bibi.jar rather than duke.jar.

The rest of the file is left as supplied. It already pins source and target
compatibility to Java 25, already declares JUnit 5 and the shadow plugin, which
the A-JUnit and A-Jar increments will use, and already wires standardInput to
the console so "gradlew run" can read commands.

Verified that "gradlew compileJava" and "gradlew run" both work, that the app
saves to ./data/bibi.txt relative to the project root under Gradle, and that the
16 UI tests still pass. The UI test runner still compiles with javac directly,
which is quicker than going through Gradle for every case and keeps the two
checks independent.

README gains a short section on building and running with the wrapper.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Gradle'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Gradle: merge the upstream add-gradle-support branch and point the build at
bibi.Bibi, so the project builds and runs through the Gradle wrapper.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests and make date parsing strict
commitResults.messageBody:
A-JUnit. 73 tests across five classes, run with "gradlew test".

Coverage follows the top ~50% highest-value methods rather than everything:

- ParserTest (20): every command word, mixed case, a command word that is only
  a prefix of another word, and each way a command can be malformed.
- StorageTest (13): the exact saved layout, a save and load round trip for all
  three task types, a missing file, a missing parent folder, blank lines, each
  kind of damaged line, and a path that is a folder rather than a file.
- TaskDateTimeTest (18): each accepted input format, formatting, storage round
  trips, and date comparison.
- TaskListTest (10): one-based numbering and its boundaries, defensive copying,
  and the unmodifiable view.
- TaskTest (12): display form, save form, occursOn, and every validation rule.

Left untested on purpose: Ui, which only writes to the console, and the thin
Command subclasses, whose behaviour is already covered through Parser and the
UI test plan.

The tests found one real bug. Java resolves dates leniently by default, so
"2019-02-30" was quietly accepted as 28 February rather than refused. The
parsing formatters now use ResolverStyle.STRICT, which required changing the
year pattern from yyyy to uuuu because the former means year-within-era and
cannot be resolved strictly on its own. A mistyped date is now reported instead
of silently becoming a different date.

AGENTS.md records the 50% coverage target, the naming convention, and that the
tests must be updated alongside each code change to stay within it.

The 16 UI tests still pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JUnit'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-JUnit: 73 JUnit 5 tests covering Parser, Storage, TaskList, TaskDateTime and
the task types, plus the strict date parsing they uncovered.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document building and running the fat JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Jar. No code or build changes were needed: the add-gradle-support branch
already brought the Shadow plugin, and A-Gradle already pointed shadowJar at
bibi.jar and disabled the lean jar task. What was missing was verification and
instructions.

Verified the scenario the increment describes: "gradlew shadowJar" produces
build/libs/bibi.jar, and copying that one file into an empty folder and running
"java -jar bibi.jar" there works with nothing else installed. The run creates
its own data/bibi.txt in that folder and a second run restores the tasks, which
confirms the relative, operating-system independent save path behaves correctly
once the app is distributed rather than run from the project.

build/ is already ignored, so the JAR is not committed. The README now explains
how to create, locate, and run it, and points at a GitHub release as the way to
publish it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Jar'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Jar: verified the shadowJar fat JAR runs standalone from an empty folder, and
documented how to create, locate, and run it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add header comments to all remaining public members
commitResults.messageBody:
Fifteen overriding methods carried no header comment: execute in each of the
eight command classes, isExit in ExitCommand, and getTypeCode and getDetails in
the three task types. Anyone reading a command class had to open Command to
learn what it does.

Each now has a summary describing what that particular class does, matching the
summary-only style the existing overrides already use. Repeating the inherited
@param tags on nine identical signatures would have added noise without adding
information.

Running the javadoc tool for the first time also exposed defects that were
invisible while compiling:

- Four {@link} references broke during A-Packages and had gone unnoticed, since
  a broken link is a javadoc error rather than a compile error. Parser, TaskList
  and Storage are now linked by qualified name with a short label, because the
  referring classes have no reason to import them just for a comment.
- Five classes relied on an implicit public constructor that no comment could
  describe. The three command classes and Command now declare documented
  constructors. Parser instead declares a private one, since it holds only
  static helpers and was never meant to be instantiated.

The javadoc task now completes with no errors and no warnings. All 73 JUnit
tests and 16 UI tests still pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Comply with the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project already shipped config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml, which
encodes the SE-EDU intermediate standard, but nothing ever ran it. The
code had therefore drifted from the standard with no way to notice.

The Gradle checkstyle plugin now applies that config, which makes
compliance verifiable rather than a matter of opinion. Its first run
reported 78 violations of three rules:

* Import order, 59 cases. Imports must be grouped as static, java, org,
  com, then this project's own classes, separated by blank lines. Almost
  every file was wrong, because imports had only ever been sorted
  alphabetically.
* Indentation, 13 cases. The case labels of the switch expression in
  Storage.parseTask sat level with the switch instead of indented
  inside it.
* Separator wrap, 6 cases. Six wrapped assertThrows calls started a line
  with the lambda's opening parenthesis, which the standard forbids.

All are fixed, and checkstyleMain and checkstyleTest now pass. The 73
JUnit tests and 16 UI tests still pass, confirming that every change was
presentational and none altered behaviour.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add seedu-java-coding-standard skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Following the coding standard is now a standing requirement, not a
one-off cleanup, so the rules need to be readable without visiting the
SE-EDU site each time.

The skill records the naming, layout, statement, and comment rules, and
points at ./gradlew checkstyleMain checkstyleTest for the parts a tool
can settle. It also notes the two things checkstyle cannot catch:
whether a name is a good name, and whether a comment is worth reading.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add seedu-git-standard skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Commit messages in this repository had no agreed shape, and the SE-EDU
Git conventions were not written down anywhere in the project.

The skill records the subject line rules, the body wrapping and content
rules, and the branch naming format, plus a short checklist to run
through before committing. It notes that the course increment branches
keep their prescribed names rather than the kebab-case convention,
because the grading scripts match on those exact names.

commitResults.messageTitle: Mandate the coding and commit standards in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
The two new skills describe the standards but nothing yet obliged anyone
to use them, so a future change could silently ignore both.

AGENTS.md now requires the Java coding standard for all code and the Git
conventions for all commit messages, names the skill that carries each,
and states that a change is unfinished while checkstyle reports
violations.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command to search task descriptions
commitResults.messageBody:
A user with a long list had no way to locate a task except to read the
whole list, which gets steadily worse as the list grows.

"find <keyword>" now shows every task whose description contains the
keyword. Two decisions worth recording:

* The match ignores case and matches any substring, so "find book"
  finds "Read Book" and "find boo" finds both. A user searching for a
  task they half remember is better served by too many results than by
  a miss on capitalisation.
* Only the description is searched, not the dates. Searching dates as
  text would make "find 2019" behave unpredictably next to the on
  command, which already answers date questions properly.

Matches keep the number they hold in the full list rather than being
renumbered from one, matching what the on command already does, so a
task found this way can be marked or removed without listing first.

Task answers hasKeyword itself, which keeps the description private and
means neither Parser nor the command needs to reach inside a task.

Covered by eight new JUnit tests and one new UI test case. Test 6 was
updated because find now appears in the unknown-command hint.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-JavaDoc'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-JavaDoc: header comments on every remaining public member, plus the
broken links and undocumented constructors the javadoc tool exposed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-CodingStandard'
Merge branch 'branch-Level-9'
commitResults.messageBody:
Level-9: find <keyword> searches task descriptions.

Git merged all three branches without a textual conflict, but this merge
still needed a fix that no tool reported.

branch-Level-9 was cut before branch-A-JavaDoc landed, so FindCommand
was written to the standard of the time and left its execute method
without a header comment. That breaks the invariant A-JavaDoc
established, that every non-private member is documented. Neither the
compiler nor checkstyle objects, because the config deliberately exempts
@Override methods, so the regression was invisible until the Javadoc
audit was rerun. The comment is added here as part of resolving the
merge, rather than in a follow-up commit, so master is never in a state
that contradicts A-JavaDoc.

The import ordering that A-CodingStandard introduced survived the merge
by luck rather than design: the find imports happened to be inserted at
alphabetically correct positions inside groups that already existed.

Verified on the merged result: checkstyle clean, javadoc clean, 81 JUnit
tests and 17 UI tests passing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Mirror the standard skills for Claude and fix VS Code settings
commitResults.messageBody:
The two standards skills lived only under .codex/skills, so only one of
the two assistants used in this project could read them. They are now
duplicated under .claude/skills, and each copy carries a note naming its
twin, because prose that exists twice drifts silently otherwise.
AGENTS.md records the same obligation.

test-ui was deliberately not duplicated. It carries a 160 line Python
script, and two copies of a script that must stay in step is a worse
trade than running it from its existing path.

.vscode/settings.json is not committed, being ignored, but is worth
recording here: it contained a syntax error. A comma was missing before
the java.checkstyle keys, so the file did not parse and none of its
settings applied, including the checkstyle configuration that was meant
to surface violations while editing. It has been rewritten with valid
JSON, the six editor settings from the SE-EDU VS Code guide, rulers at
110 and 120 to make the line limits visible, and Gradle import enabled.
The java.project.sourcePaths and java.project.outputPath entries were
dropped, since they apply only to unmanaged folders and have been inert
since this became a Gradle project.
